title: “When Hope Didn’t Stop: Terry’s Marathon of Faith”
paragraphs: “When Hope Didn’t Stop: Terry’s Marathon of Faith”
He ran 5,373 km for a dream bigger than himself — and ours now.”

On 28 July 1958, in Winnipeg, Canada, a boy named Terry Fox was born. Active and competitive, Terry grew up loving sport and movement, until in 1977 he was diagnosed with osteogenic sarcoma, a bone cancer. He lost his right leg—amputated above the knee—and yet his spirit refused to take a seat on the sidelines.
In hospital, he watched fellow cancer patients, especially children, suffering and waiting. A fire lit within him. Not just to survive—but to serve.

Many would have withdrawn into fear and pain. But Terry turned his pain into purpose. He set his sights on something audacious: to run across Canada. He named it the “Marathon of Hope.” He began training, hopping along on his prosthetic leg, each step a statement: “I may be limited, but I am not defeated.”
On 12 April 1980, Terry dipped his prosthetic leg into the Atlantic Ocean at St. John’s, Newfoundland—his official start line. He embarked on daily marathons, averaging 26 miles (42 km) a day, through wind and rain, through pain that we can barely imagine.

But halfway through, the fear loomed: his cancer returned. On 1 September 1980, after 143 days and 5,373 km of running, Terry was forced to stop outside Thunder Bay—his body saying “enough” though his heart still said “go”.

What’s remarkable is not only what Terry did, but what he left behind. Although he died on 28 June 1981, aged only 22, his vision lived on. He had raised millions for cancer research, but more than that, he sparked a movement. The annual Terry Fox Run now spans dozens of countries, with over C$800 million raised worldwide for cancer research.

What began as a young man’s bold race became a journey for the human family. Terry’s simple message: don’t wait until you feel strong; begin now. Don’t wait for perfect; move with what you have.
From a faith-driven perspective, Terry embodied the truth that our “weakness may become a stage for grace.” His one leg, his broken body, were not the ends—they were the launching pad.

Today, you and I can carry forward that legacy. We might not run across countries, but we can run the race set before us: working with courage, loving with open hands, believing in more than our limitations.

In our own “marathons”—be it illness, job loss, relation broken—we can remember: a single step followed by another becomes momentum. Terry didn’t say: “When I’m healed I will serve.” He said: “I must run now.”
In our faith language: When our body is frail, the Spirit is strong. When our resources are scant, compassion deepens. When our time is short—our impact can endure.

Imagine a child in Manila or Cebu, hearing Terry’s story and believing: If he could run for hope, I can walk for change. Imagine a community rallying around someone sick, not simply surviving—but becoming the next echo of hope.
Terry’s legacy invites us: dream bold, run steady, believe bigger. His one leg lost did not stop the journey. Your one possibility lost does not stop yours.
So today, take your next step—toward someone needing hope, toward a dream needing your stride, toward faith unfolding in action.
🕊 Moral / Takeaway
In weakness we find our strength in Christ. Terry teaches us that faith moves feet.
Hope thrives when we turn limitations into service—and our pain becomes purpose.
Your challenges need not limit you—they can lead you. Hope keeps running.
🗣 Shareable Quote
“I lost my leg, not my purpose.” – Terry Fox
“When was the last time you turned a limitation into a purpose?”

“Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, fixing our eyes on Jesus.”
— Hebrews 12 : 1-2 (ESV)
